original_question: For the same radial Riesz equilibrium problem with -2 < s < d and alpha > max{0, -s}, determine exactly when the support of the equilibrium measure is full dimensional in R^d and when it has dimension strictly smaller than d.
target_in_paper: Section 1, Question 1.2 (Robert Womersley, Edward Saff), in the immediate context of Theorem 1.1 and the surrounding discussion on dimension reduction for radial Riesz equilibrium measures. The notation and the sharp sphere-support threshold that this question builds on are supplied by the cited paper [1], especially its setup in §1.1 and Theorem 1.3. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2504.04845))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the right topic: the full-space radial Riesz equilibrium problem on R^d, the power-law external field regime with -2 < s < d and alpha > max{0,-s}, and the specific issue of support dimension rather than merely the already-solved question of when the support is exactly a sphere. That matches the intent of Question 1.2, which asks when the equilibrium support is full dimensional versus lower dimensional. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2504.04845))
missing_details: The paper’s equilibrium problem should be stated explicitly: minimize I_{s,V}(mu) = ∬(K_s(x-y) + V(x) + V(y)) dmu(x) dmu(y) over probability measures mu on R^d.
The kernel normalization used in the underlying source [1] is K_s(x) = 1/(s ||x||^s) for s != 0 and K_0(x) = -log ||x||; your draft leaves the operator/kernel implicit.
The ambient dimension restriction d >= 2 is part of the setup in [1].
The external field should be named explicitly as the power-law field V(x) = (gamma/alpha) ||x||^alpha with gamma > 0; your draft omits gamma entirely.

To stay closest to the paper, the question should be tied to the regime left open after the sphere-support classification: for -2 < s < d - 3, Theorem 1.3 in [1] already settles alpha >= alpha_{s,d}, so the unresolved issue is what happens outside the known spherical-support regime.

The phrase "full dimensional" is left implicit in the draft; the nearby discussion suggests the intended contrast is between support having a full-dimensional component in R^d and support lying on a set of dimension < d.

Your draft does not mention the nearby motivating cases recorded in the paper: earlier examples with ball/sphere-type lower-dimensional support, and the cited case where the equilibrium measure has a full-dimensional component.

The paper’s section 1 first treats general radial fields V(x) = v(||x||^2), then specializes in Theorem 1.1/[1, Theorem 1.3] to power laws; a stand-alone version should make clear that it is the power-law specialization that is being asked about.
refined_question: Consider the full-space Riesz equilibrium problem on R^d, d >= 2, with kernel K_s(x) = 1/(s ||x||^s) for s != 0 and K_0(x) = -log ||x||, and with power-law radial external field V(x) = (gamma/alpha) ||x||^alpha, where gamma > 0, -2 < s < d, and alpha > max{-s,0}. Let mu_eq be the equilibrium measure minimizing I_{s,V}(mu) = ∬(K_s(x-y) + V(x) + V(y)) dmu(x) dmu(y) over probability measures on R^d. After the sharp classification of the spherical-support regime given in Theorem 1.1 of this section (equivalently, [1, Theorem 1.3]), determine for which parameter choices (d,s,alpha) the support supp(mu_eq) has a full-dimensional component in R^d, and for which parameter choices supp(mu_eq) is supported on a set of dimension strictly smaller than d. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2504.04845))
justification: The nearest official target is not a conjecture or theorem but Question 1.2 in §1 of arXiv:2504.04845: "When is the support of the equilibrium measure full dimensional and when is the support of dimension less than d?" The preceding text says that Theorem 1.1 characterizes when the support is a sphere and then asks whether dimension reduction occurs for other combinations of alpha and s; it also records a known case where the equilibrium measure has a full-dimensional component. In the cited source [1], the same setup is written out precisely: §1.1 defines the kernel, the energy, and radial fields V(x)=v(||x||^2), while Theorem 1.3 specializes to V(x)=(gamma/alpha)||x||^alpha and gives the sharp threshold alpha_{s,d} for the spherical-support case; Theorem 1.2 supplies nearby structural information when s >= d-3. So your draft is directionally right, but it is not fully stand-alone or fully paper-faithful until it states the energy, kernel normalization, gamma, and the relation to the already-settled spherical-support regime. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2504.04845))
